newsitem.title: FRANCE: French by-election tests left, right weaknesses.
newsitem.headline: French by-election tests left, right weaknesses.

text.p: A by-election to replace bankrupt business mogul Bernard Tapie in parliament, fought out in a depressed working-class town near Marseille, is set to test the weaknesses of France's mainstream Left and Right on Sunday.

Tapie won the seat in 1993 for the small left-wing Radical movement, since renamed the Radical Socialist Party. At the time, he was boss of the successful Marseille soccer club and minister of urban affairs in a Socialist-led government.
The fast-talking entrepreneur hardly ever returned to his constituency and has since been stripped of his seat after being ruled bankrupt and convicted of fraud, tax evasion and bribery.

His party has picked as its candidate another national political celebrity, former health and humanitarian action minister Bernard Kouchner, with the backing of the mainstream opposition Socialist Party, but local residents are deeply suspicious.

"We voted for Tapie in 1993 and never saw him again. Now they're trying the same thing with Kouchner. Even if he gets elected, he knows nothing about people's problems here," said a waiter at a bar in the village of Bouc-bel-Air.

Kouchner, known internationally as a founder of the medical relief group Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors without Borders), showed almost total ignorance of the constituency in a debate with fellow candidates, admitting he did not even know the names of the districts in Gardanne.
His suave Parisian intellectual oratory ill equips him for the rough-and-tumble of Provencal politics.
That should have helped his mainstream conservative opponent, Herve Fabre-Aubrespy, defeated by Tapie in 1993, who has the advantage of being from the region.

But he has his own problems. Although he is the official candidate of the ruling centre-right RPR-UDF coalition, no national leaders have turned out to support him because he is a follower of maverick right-wing Eurosceptic Philippe de Villiers, an outspoken critic of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
Local conservative leaders, including Marseille mayor and Regional Development Minister Jean-Claude Gaudin, are enemies.

So two outsiders could have a chance of stealing the show in Sunday's first ballot: Communist Roger Mei, a local mayor with deep roots in the constituency, and extreme-right National Front candidate Damien Bariller.
Their supporters squared off for a major round of fisticuffs in the centre of Gardanne on Thursday in which seven people were hurt.

Both sides feed on fears about unemployment -- the coal mine that is Gardanne's biggest employer with 4,000 jobs is due to close in 2005 -- and immigration, especially after recent incidents of racial violence in neighbouring Marseille.
Mei has garnered support from some Socialist notables, including Edmonde Charles-Roux, the widow of legendary Marseille mayor Gaston Defferre.
Bariller is hoping to improve on the 17 percent of the vote he won in 1993. National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen plans to give him a boost by addressing his final campaign rally.
So the outcome is highly uncertain and a Communist-National Front run-off in a week's time is a distinct possibility.
That would be an embarrassment for both France's mainstream political families 18 months before the 1998 general election, suggesting that neither has an answer to voters' main concerns.
